write.desc: Uniform continuity strengthens continuity by making delta depend on epsilon alone, not on the point; its points belong together because they all work with that single change in quantifier order: how to prove it, how to disprove it, the Lipschitz condition that gives it cheaply, the Heine-Cantor theorem that gives it for free on compact sets, and its use in preserving Cauchy sequences and extending functions to endpoints.

points.name: Uniform continuity versus continuity: the order of the quantifiers
points.what: The learner can state the definition of uniform continuity on a set A and write it side by side with continuity at every point of A, seeing that the only change is moving 'for all x' after 'there exists delta', so delta may depend on epsilon but not on the point. They can explain why uniform continuity implies continuity and not the reverse.
outside: epsilon-delta definition of continuity at a point and on a set
how the order of nested quantifiers changes the meaning of a statement (for all / there exists)

points.name: Negating uniform continuity
points.what: The learner can write out correctly what it means for f not to be uniformly continuous on A: there is an epsilon_0 > 0 such that for every delta > 0 there are x, y in A with |x - y| < delta and |f(x) - f(y)| >= epsilon_0, and can compare it with the negation of continuity at a point.

points.name: Proving uniform continuity from the definition
points.what: The learner can do the scratch work and write a proof that a given function is uniformly continuous by finding a delta depending only on epsilon, for example x^2 on [0,1] (delta = epsilon/2), 1/x on [1, infinity) (delta = epsilon) and sqrt x on [0, infinity) (using |sqrt x - sqrt y| <= sqrt|x - y|, delta = epsilon^2).

points.name: Sequential criterion for failure of uniform continuity
points.what: The learner can state and prove that f fails to be uniformly continuous on A exactly when there are an epsilon_0 > 0 and sequences (x_n), (y_n) in A with x_n - y_n -> 0 but |f(x_n) - f(y_n)| >= epsilon_0 for all n, and knows this is the usual tool for disproving uniform continuity.
outside: convergence of a sequence of real numbers

points.name: Disproving uniform continuity: x^2 on R and 1/x on (0,1)
points.what: The learner can prove that x^2 is not uniformly continuous on R (take x_n = n + 1/n, y_n = n) and 1/x is not uniformly continuous on (0,1) (take x_n = 1/n, y_n = 1/(n+1)), and can say what goes wrong in each case: unbounded steepness at infinity, or blow-up near a missing endpoint.

points.name: Lipschitz functions
points.what: The learner can define a Lipschitz function (|f(x) - f(y)| <= K|x - y|), prove that Lipschitz implies uniformly continuous with delta = epsilon/K, and show the converse fails with sqrt x on [0, infinity), which is uniformly continuous but not Lipschitz because its difference quotients near 0 are unbounded.

points.name: The Heine-Cantor theorem
points.what: The learner can state and prove that a continuous function on a compact set (for example a closed bounded interval [a,b]) is uniformly continuous, by contradiction: build sequences from the negation, extract convergent subsequences with Bolzano-Weierstrass, and use continuity at the common limit. They can point to the examples 1/x on (0,1) and x^2 on R to show why closedness and boundedness are needed, and know this theorem is what later makes continuous functions Riemann integrable.
outside: Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem: every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence
compact sets of R (closed and bounded, sequential compactness)

points.name: Uniformly continuous functions preserve Cauchy sequences
points.what: The learner can prove that if f is uniformly continuous on A and (x_n) is a Cauchy sequence in A then (f(x_n)) is Cauchy, and can show this fails for merely continuous functions with 1/x on (0,1) and x_n = 1/n.
outside: Cauchy sequences and the Cauchy criterion for convergence

points.name: Continuous extension to the endpoints
points.what: The learner can prove that a uniformly continuous function on (a,b) has limits at a and b and so extends to a continuous function on [a,b], using that it maps Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences, and with Heine-Cantor can conclude that a continuous function on (a,b) is uniformly continuous exactly when it extends continuously to [a,b] (so sin(1/x) on (0,1) is not uniformly continuous).
outside: sequential criterion for limits of functions

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd ed., Springer)
where.detail: Section 4.4, Continuous Functions on Compact Sets (uniform continuity, sequential criterion, Theorem 4.4.7) and its exercises on extension and Lipschitz functions

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis
where.detail: Section 5.4, Uniform Continuity (Lipschitz functions, Uniform Continuity Theorem, Continuous Extension Theorem)
